text: ISNULL and COALESCE look interchangeable at first glance — both replace a NULL with a fallback value, and on a simple case like this one they produce identical output. The real differences only show up once you look past the surface.

First difference: ISNULL never takes more than two arguments. COALESCE can chain as many fallback candidates as you need in one flat call. To get the same three-way fallback out of ISNULL, you have to nest one call inside another.

Here's the real gotcha, and a genuinely classic interview question. ISNULL's result type is based on its FIRST argument's declared type, no matter what the second argument is. Declare a five-character VARCHAR, pass it as the first argument with a much longer fallback string, and ISNULL silently truncates that fallback down to five characters. No error, no warning — it just quietly cuts it off.

COALESCE avoids that trap entirely, because it follows standard data type precedence across ALL of its arguments, not just the first. The result type ends up wide enough to hold the longer string untouched. Same two values, very different outcome.

One more distinction worth knowing: COALESCE is part of the ANSI SQL standard, so the same expression behaves consistently on Oracle, Postgres, and other ANSI databases. ISNULL is T-SQL only — SQL Server's own function, with no identical equivalent elsewhere.

So: two arguments and a type inherited from the first one, versus any number of arguments with standard type precedence. Next up, a function that does something almost the opposite of both — NULLIF, which turns a matching value INTO a NULL on purpose.
